group.passage:
One tourist is in New York to attend a concert but gets lost. He spots a man carrying a violin case. “Sir, can you tell me how to get to Carnegie Hall?” The musician smiles and says, “Practice, practice, practice.”
Celebrating its 132nd birthday this year, Carnegie Hall is the aspirational destination for the world’s best musicians, as well as a synonym of international standard for musical excellence. Among the things that make Carnegie Hall the <u>holy grail</u> of musical performance is its stunning acoustics. In fact, were it not for the unparalleled beautiful sound, this venue could have long been demolished.
As principal architect, William Burnet Tuthill is generally credited with the acoustics. He sought advice and guidance from his contemporary musicians and architects of prestigious music halls, such as Dankmar Adler, who designed the acoustics for Chicago Auditorium Theatre. An amateur cellist and lacking in experience in building a concert hall, Tuthill sent out a questionnaire to hundreds of concert halls all over the world to survey what shapes and structural features had the most impact on concert sound. His brainchild—the Hall’s smooth interior design, oval shape, extended stage, and domed ceiling—helps project both soft and loud tones to any location in the Hall with equal clarity and richness.
Reigning almost supreme among music halls, Carnegie Hall was not without rivals. As the U.S. <u>emerged</u> triumphant from World War Two, a fad, and almost a race, of concert hall construction began. In the late 1950s, the New York Philharmonic left Carnegie Hall to relocate in the recently constructed Lincoln Center. Dealt a <u>heavy blow</u>, Carnegie Hall was planned to be taken down as it was no longer a reliable source of profit. Isaac Stern, a prominent and respected violinist, led a campaign to remind everyone of the Hall’s historical significance. He <u>rallied</u> his fellow musicians and the musical public, demonstrated in their concerts the magnificent sound of the Hall, and launched a successful operation to rescue the Hall by convincing New York City to purchase the building. Today, Carnegie Hall’s prestige, along with its brilliant acoustics, towers in the world of music appreciation.

questions.stem: Of the underlined words or phrases, which of the following pairs of synonyms is correct?

Based on this article, what would be the correct sequence of description for the following sentences (1)~(4), T(true), F(false), or NG(not given)?
(1) Dankmar Adler designed a famous building.
(2) Most New Yorkers don’t know where the Carnegie Hall is.
(3) Isaac Stern was an advocate for the Hall’s demolishment.
(4) The Hall once failed to attract enough performance and audience.
